decks.title: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation — Part 1: Mixtures, solutions and concentration
goals: Classify mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous
Distinguish solutions, suspensions and colloids by particle size, stability, filtration and the Tyndall effect
Calculate concentration as mass percentage, volume percentage and mass by volume
Interpret solubility graphs and explain crystallisation on cooling

slides.heading: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation
slides.body_md: Part 1: what is a mixture, how a solution differs from a suspension and a colloid, how strong a solution is, and how much of a solid water can hold.

visual.alt: Table of six everyday materials sorted into pure substances and mixtures

slides.narration: Almost everything around us, from the tea in a cup to the air in a classroom, is a mixture. In this part we learn how to sort mixtures, how to tell a solution from a suspension and a colloid, how to say how strong a solution is, and how the amount of a solid that dissolves changes with temperature.

slides.heading: Pure substances and mixtures
slides.body_md: A **pure substance** has a fixed composition and fixed properties, such as a sharp melting point. Elements and compounds are pure substances. A **mixture** has two or more substances mixed **physically**, in **any proportion**, and each keeps its own properties. A mixture can be separated by physical means.

visual.alt: Flow chart: matter divides into pure substances (elements and compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous and heterogeneous)
visual.caption: Classification of matter

slides.narration: Matter can be a pure substance or a mixture. A pure substance has a fixed makeup, like gold or distilled water. It may be an element or a compound. A mixture has two or more substances mixed in any proportion without a chemical change, so each one keeps its own properties. Because of that, we can separate the parts of a mixture by simple physical methods.

slides.heading: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
slides.body_md: In a **homogeneous mixture** the composition is uniform throughout, so you cannot see separate parts. In a **heterogeneous mixture** the composition varies from place to place and the parts can often be seen. Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is a homogeneous mixture: it is a **solid solution**.

rows: solid solution of copper and zinc
mud particles can be seen and settle

visual.alt: Table classifying six mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous with the reason

slides.narration: In a homogeneous mixture the makeup is the same everywhere. Sugar syrup, air without dust and brass are examples. In a heterogeneous mixture the makeup changes from place to place, and often you can see the parts. Muddy river water, sand mixed with iron filings, and oil floating on water are examples. Brass is a solid solution of copper and zinc.

slides.narration: Quick check. Think about whether a uniform looking metal made by melting two metals together is a compound or a mixture, and of which kind.

slides.heading: How big are the particles?
slides.body_md: The three kinds of liquid mixtures differ mainly in **particle size**. In a true **solution** the particles are smaller than about 1 nm. In a **colloid** they are between about 1 nm and 1000 nm. In a **suspension** they are bigger than about 1000 nm, large enough to see and to settle.

slides.narration: The main difference between a solution, a colloid and a suspension is the size of the particles. In a true solution, they are smaller than about one nanometre, so small that they never settle and cannot be seen. In a colloid they lie between one nanometre and one thousand nanometres. In a suspension, they are bigger still, so they can be seen and slowly settle.

slides.heading: Solution, suspension and colloid compared
slides.body_md: A **solution** is clear and stable. A **suspension** is cloudy, its particles settle on standing and are caught by filter paper. A **colloid** looks uniform, is stable and does not settle, passes through ordinary filter paper (but not through very fine membranes such as parchment) and scatters light.

rows: yes, if the liquid is not too opaque

visual.alt: Table comparing solutions, colloids and suspensions on five properties

slides.narration: Here is the comparison. A solution is clear, never settles, and passes through filter paper. A suspension is cloudy, its particles settle on standing, and filter paper holds them back as a residue. A colloid looks uniform and does not settle. It also passes through ordinary filter paper, but it scatters a beam of light, and that is how we recognise it.

slides.heading: The Tyndall effect
slides.body_md: When a beam of light passes through a colloid, the particles are big enough to **scatter** it, so the path of the beam shows up. This is the **Tyndall effect**. A true solution does not scatter light. The sunbeams you see slanting through a forest on a misty morning are the same effect: tiny water droplets and dust scatter the sunlight.

slides.narration: Shine a torch through three beakers. In the salt solution the beam passes without being seen inside the liquid. In dilute milk, the path of the beam shines clearly, because the colloid particles scatter the light. This is the Tyndall effect. Sunbeams slanting through a misty forest show the same thing, with tiny water droplets and dust scattering the light.

slides.heading: Colloids in everyday life
slides.body_md: Colloids are named by what is spread (the **dispersed phase**) and what it is spread in (the **dispersion medium**). Common kinds at this level are **aerosols**, **foams**, **emulsions**, **sols** and **gels**.

visual.alt: Table of five colloid types with what is dispersed in what and two examples each

slides.narration: Colloids are named by what is spread and what it is spread in. Fog and smoke are aerosols, with tiny drops or specks in air. Shaving cream is a foam, with gas bubbles in liquid. Milk and face cream are emulsions, with liquid spread in liquid. Ink and paint are sols, solid in liquid. Jelly and cheese are gels, with liquid held in a solid.

slides.heading: Worked example: what kind of mixture is it?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Three liquids A, B and C are tested. Identify each.

**Step 1.** A is clear, never settles, leaves nothing on the filter paper and shows no beam: a **solution**.

**Step 2.** B is cloudy, settles in an hour and leaves a residue on the filter paper: a **suspension**.

**Step 3.** C looks uniform, does not settle, passes through the filter paper but shows a bright beam: a **colloid**.

visual.alt: Table of three liquids and the results of settling, filtering and beam tests with the verdict for each

slides.narration: Let us test three liquids. Liquid A is clear, does not settle, leaves nothing on the filter paper and shows no beam, so it is a solution. Liquid B is cloudy, settles in an hour and leaves a residue, so it is a suspension. Liquid C looks uniform, does not settle and passes through the paper, but it shows a bright beam, so it is a colloid.

slides.heading: How strong is a solution?
slides.body_md:
The **solute** dissolves in the **solvent** to make the **solution**. The **concentration** says how much solute is present. At this level there are three common ways.

$$\text{mass percentage} = \dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$$
$$\text{volume percentage} = \dfrac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}} \times 100$$
$$\text{mass by volume percentage} = \dfrac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (mL)}} \times 100$$

rows: a solid is dissolved to a measured volume

visual.alt: Table of three ways of stating concentration, when each is used and an example

slides.narration: The solute dissolves in the solvent to make the solution. To say how strong a solution is, we state its concentration. Mass percentage is the mass of solute divided by the mass of the whole solution, times one hundred. Volume percentage does the same with volumes, for liquids. Mass by volume uses grams of solute in a measured volume of solution, in millilitres.

slides.heading: Worked example: mass percentage
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A sweet seller dissolves 36 g of sugar in 164 g of water. Find the mass percentage of sugar.

**Step 1: mass of solution** $= 36 + 164 = 200$ g.

**Step 2:** $\dfrac{36}{200} \times 100 = 18\ \%$.

visual.alt: Table of the masses of sugar, water and solution and the mass percentage

slides.narration: A sweet seller dissolves thirty six grams of sugar in one hundred and sixty four grams of water. First find the mass of the solution, by adding solute and solvent. That is two hundred grams. Then divide the mass of sugar by the mass of solution and multiply by one hundred. We get eighteen percent. Do not divide by the mass of water alone.

slides.heading: Worked example: volume percentage and mass by volume
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A student makes 80 mL of a drink using 12 mL of lemon juice. Find the volume percentage. (b) 9 g of salt is dissolved to make 150 mL of solution. Find the mass by volume percentage.

**(a)** $\dfrac{12}{80} \times 100 = 15\ \%$.

**(b)** $\dfrac{9}{150} \times 100 = 6.0\ \%$ (mass by volume).

visual.alt: Table of the two worked cases with solute, solution and concentration

slides.narration: Two quick cases. In the first, twelve millilitres of lemon juice make eighty millilitres of drink, so the volume percentage is twelve divided by eighty, times one hundred, which is fifteen percent. In the second, nine grams of salt make one hundred and fifty millilitres of solution, so the mass by volume percentage is six percent.

slides.heading: Solubility, saturated and unsaturated solutions
slides.body_md: The **solubility** of a substance is the maximum mass of it that dissolves in **100 g of solvent** at a given temperature. A solution that can still dissolve more solute at that temperature is **unsaturated**. One that holds the maximum is **saturated**: any extra solute stays undissolved.

visual.alt: Table explaining unsaturated and saturated solutions and solubility

slides.narration: Solubility is the largest mass of a substance that dissolves in one hundred grams of solvent at a given temperature. A solution that can still take more solute is unsaturated. A solution that already holds the largest amount is saturated, and any extra solute you add just stays at the bottom. Solubility depends on the substance, the solvent and the temperature.

slides.heading: Reading solubility curves
slides.body_md: A **solubility curve** plots solubility against temperature. The values here are **approximate and illustrative**. Potassium nitrate rises steeply with temperature, while sodium chloride is nearly flat. Any point **on** a curve is a saturated solution, a point **below** it is unsaturated.

visual.caption: Approximate, illustrative solubility curves.

slides.narration: Look at the curves. The red curve shows potassium nitrate. Its solubility rises steeply as the water gets hotter. The blue curve shows common salt, which hardly changes with temperature. A point on a curve means a saturated solution. A point below the curve means an unsaturated solution. These values are approximate and used only for practice in reading graphs.

slides.heading: Worked example: crystals on cooling
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A saturated solution of potassium nitrate is made with 200 g of water at 60 °C and cooled to 30 °C. How much crystallises? Use the curve.

**Step 1.** At 60 °C: $110 \times 2 = 220$ g dissolve in 200 g of water.

**Step 2.** At 30 °C: $46 \times 2 = 92$ g can stay dissolved.

**Step 3.** Crystals $= 220 - 92 = 128$ g.

visual.alt: Table of the mass of potassium nitrate dissolved at 60 and 30 degrees Celsius for 100 and 200 grams of water and the difference

slides.narration: We make a saturated solution with two hundred grams of water at sixty degrees Celsius and cool it to thirty degrees. From the curve, one hundred grams of water holds one hundred and ten grams at sixty degrees and forty six grams at thirty degrees. For two hundred grams of water, double these. The difference, one hundred and twenty eight grams, comes out as crystals.

slides.heading: Temperature, gases and crystallisation
slides.body_md: For most solids, solubility **rises** with temperature, so a hot saturated solution gives crystals when it **cools**: this is **crystallisation**, used to get pure copper sulphate or alum crystals. For **gases** it is the opposite: solubility **falls** when the temperature rises. This is why warm water holds less dissolved oxygen for fish, and why a warm fizzy drink loses its gas quickly.

rows: more sugar dissolves in hot tea

visual.alt: Table showing how heating affects the solubility of most solids, sodium chloride and gases with an everyday sign

slides.narration: For most solids, solubility rises with temperature, so a hot saturated solution gives crystals as it cools. That is crystallisation. Common salt is an exception, because its solubility barely changes. For gases, the effect is the opposite. Warm water holds less dissolved gas. That is why bubbles escape from a warm fizzy drink, and why fish struggle in very warm ponds.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: A pure substance has fixed composition; a mixture has variable composition and is separable by physical means.
Homogeneous mixtures are uniform; heterogeneous mixtures show visible parts.
Solutions (below 1 nm) are clear and stable; colloids (1 to 1000 nm) scatter light; suspensions (above 1000 nm) settle and are filtered off.
Mass percentage uses the mass of the whole solution; volume percentage and mass by volume use volumes.
Solubility is grams per 100 g of solvent; most solids dissolve more in hot water, so cooling a saturated solution gives crystals.

visual.alt: Table summarising the key point for five ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up. A mixture has variable makeup and can be separated by physical means. Solutions are clear and stable, colloids scatter light and do not settle, and suspensions settle. Concentration is solute divided by solution, times one hundred. Solubility is the grams that saturate one hundred grams of solvent, and cooling a hot saturated solution gives crystals.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Divide by the mass of the whole solution, not the mass of the solvent.
Write the formula, then the numbers with units, then the percentage sign.
To identify a colloid, quote the Tyndall effect and that it does not settle.
When reading a curve, draw dashed guide lines to the axes and quote both values.
Say whether a point lies on a curve (saturated) or below it (unsaturated).
slides.narration: Some exam tips. When you find a percentage, divide by the mass of the whole solution, not just the solvent. Write the formula first, then substitute with units. To prove a liquid is a colloid, mention that it does not settle and that it scatters a beam of light. On a solubility graph, draw guide lines to both axes and read both values.

decks.title: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation — Part 2: Separation techniques
goals: Explain evaporation, crystallisation, distillation, chromatography and centrifugation
Choose a method from the property that differs between the components
Relate the methods to salt pans, butter churning, winnowing, attars and jaggery

slides.heading: Separation techniques
slides.body_md: Part 2: a mixture can be split into its parts by physical methods. The skill is to pick the property that differs.

visual.alt: Table of five mixtures, the property that differs and the method used

slides.narration: To separate a mixture we must find a property in which its parts differ. Salt does not evaporate but water does. Two liquids may boil at different temperatures. Dyes travel at different speeds on paper. Cream is lighter than skim milk, and husk is lighter than grain. Each difference leads us to a method, and we will meet them all in this part.

slides.heading: Choosing a method
slides.body_md: Ask three questions. **Is it a solid in a liquid?** If the solid has settled or is a suspension, use decantation or filtration; if it is dissolved, use evaporation or crystallisation. **Are both liquids?** If they mix, use distillation; if they form layers, use a separating funnel. **Are both solids?** Use a property such as magnetism, sublimation, size or weight.

nodes.label: Solid in liquid: evaporation, crystallisation, filtration, decantation, centrifugation
Two liquids: distillation or separating funnel
Solid with solid: magnet, sublimation, sieving, winnowing

visual.alt: Flow chart of the kind of mixture leading to a group of separation methods
visual.caption: Choosing a method

slides.narration: First ask what kind of mixture it is. A solid mixed in a liquid may need evaporation, crystallisation, filtration or centrifugation. Two liquids need distillation if they mix, or a separating funnel if they form layers. Two solids need a property that differs, such as magnetism, sublimation, size or weight. And a mixture of many dyes is a job for chromatography.

slides.heading: Evaporation and the salt pans of Gujarat
slides.body_md: **Evaporation** separates a **dissolved solid** from its liquid: heat or sunshine turns the liquid into vapour and the solid is left behind. On the Gujarat coast, sea water is led into wide shallow pans. Sun and wind evaporate the water over days, and common salt is left as a crust, which is then raked up and washed. Salt pans use sunlight, so no fuel is needed.

rows: shallow pans fill from the sea
water evaporates and the brine gets stronger
salt separates as the brine becomes saturated
salt is raked, washed and dried

visual.alt: Table of four stages of salt making in a salt pan

slides.narration: Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from its liquid. On the Gujarat coast, sea water is let into wide shallow pans. Sun and wind slowly evaporate the water, and the brine becomes stronger. When it is saturated, common salt separates as a crust. It is raked up, washed and dried. The method needs no fuel, only sunlight, wind and patience.

slides.heading: Crystallisation, and jaggery
slides.body_md: Heating a solution until **all** the water evaporates can spoil the solid and leave impurities in it. **Crystallisation** is better: evaporate part of the water to get a hot, nearly saturated solution, then let it **cool slowly**. Pure crystals form and the impurities stay in the liquid. Sugar cane juice is boiled to thicken it, and as the thick syrup cools, sugar crystals form: this is how traditional **jaggery** is set.

visual.alt: Table comparing evaporation to dryness and crystallisation on four points

slides.narration: If we boil away all the water, the solid may char and impurities remain mixed in it. Crystallisation is gentler. We evaporate only part of the water, then let the hot solution cool slowly. Pure crystals form while impurities stay in the liquid. Sugar cane juice is boiled and thickened, and as the syrup cools, sugar crystals form, giving jaggery.

slides.heading: Simple distillation
slides.body_md: **Distillation** separates two liquids, or a liquid from a dissolved solid, using a difference in **boiling point**. The mixture is heated. The more volatile part boils first, its vapour passes through a **condenser** cooled by water entering at the **lower** end, and the liquid, the **distillate**, drips into the receiver. The thermometer bulb is level with the side arm to read the temperature of the vapour.

visual.caption: Simple distillation.

slides.narration: In simple distillation the mixture is heated in a flask. The part with the lower boiling point turns to vapour first. The vapour passes into a condenser, where cold water flowing in at the lower end cools it back into liquid. The liquid, called the distillate, drips into the receiving flask. The thermometer bulb sits level with the side arm, so it reads the temperature of the vapour.

slides.heading: Worked example: separating acetone and water
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A mixture of acetone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C) is distilled. Describe what happens.

**Step 1.** Heat slowly. Acetone boils first, so the thermometer stays near **56 °C** while acetone vapour passes into the condenser.

**Step 2.** The first distillate is nearly pure acetone. When it is mostly gone, the temperature **rises** towards 100 °C.

**Step 3.** Change the receiver. What now distils is mainly water. The large gap of 44 °C makes **simple distillation** enough.

visual.alt: Table of the thermometer reading and the distillate at three stages of distilling acetone and water

slides.narration: Suppose we distil a mixture of acetone and water. Acetone boils at fifty six degrees Celsius and water at one hundred. On heating, the thermometer stays near fifty six while acetone vapour is condensed. Then the temperature rises. We change the receiver, and later water distils at about one hundred degrees. A gap of forty four degrees is large enough for simple distillation.

slides.heading: Fractional distillation
slides.body_md: When the boiling points are **close**, simple distillation is not enough. A **fractionating column**, packed with glass beads, is fitted between the flask and the condenser. Vapour condenses and re-evaporates again and again on the beads, and each time it becomes richer in the more volatile liquid. Examples: ethanol and water, the gases of **liquefied air**, and the fractions of **petroleum**.

visual.alt: Table of three mixtures separated by fractional distillation with the reason and the parts obtained

slides.narration: If two liquids have close boiling points, simple distillation is not enough. We then use a fractionating column between the flask and the condenser. Vapour condenses and evaporates again and again inside it, becoming richer in the more volatile liquid each time. This method separates ethanol from water, the gases in liquefied air, and the different fractions of petroleum.

slides.heading: Attars of Kannauj: the deg and bhapka
slides.body_md: In Kannauj, attar makers distil fragrant flowers by a traditional method. Flower petals and water are heated in a large copper pot, the **deg**. The scented vapour travels through a bamboo pipe into a copper receiver, the **bhapka**, standing in a cool water tank, where it condenses. Oils from the flowers are then collected, traditionally in a base of sandalwood oil. It is the same idea as distillation: heat, vapour, cool, collect.

This traditional method works on the same idea as a laboratory distillation: heat, vapour, cool and collect.

slides.body_md:
**Chromatography** separates substances that move at **different speeds**. A spot of the sample is placed on a **pencil** base line on paper, and the paper stands in a solvent. The solvent rises, carrying each substance a different distance. Compare spots with known dyes, and compute the $R_f$ value.

$$R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent front}}$$

slides.narration: In paper chromatography, we place a spot of the sample on a pencil line near the bottom of a paper strip, and stand the paper in a solvent. The solvent rises and carries each substance a different distance. We compare the spots with known dyes. The R f value is the distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent front. It has no unit and is always less than one.

slides.heading: Worked example: Rf values
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The solvent front rose 9.0 cm. Two spots of a leaf extract rose 3.6 cm and 6.3 cm. Find the $R_f$ of each.

**Step 1.** $R_f = \dfrac{3.6}{9.0} = 0.40$.

**Step 2.** $R_f = \dfrac{6.3}{9.0} = 0.70$.

Both are between 0 and 1. The substance with the larger $R_f$ travelled faster.

slides.narration: The solvent front rose nine centimetres. The first spot of a leaf extract rose three point six centimetres, so its R f is three point six divided by nine, which is zero point four. The second spot rose six point three centimetres, so its R f is zero point seven. Both lie between zero and one, and the second pigment moved faster.

slides.heading: Centrifugation
slides.body_md: A **centrifuge** spins a mixture fast. The heavier, denser particles are flung to the **bottom** of the tube as **sediment**, and the lighter liquid stays above. It separates fine suspended particles that settle too slowly or pass through filter paper. Uses: blood cells from plasma in a pathology lab, and **cream from milk** in a cream separator. Tubes are always placed in opposite pairs so that the rotor stays balanced.

slides.narration: A centrifuge spins tubes very fast. The denser particles are flung outward, to the bottom of each tube, where they collect as sediment. The lighter liquid stays above. Hospitals use it to separate blood cells from plasma. A cream separator uses it on milk. Tubes are always placed in opposite pairs, so that the rotor spins steadily without wobbling.

slides.heading: Butter from curd and cream from milk
slides.body_md: Milk is an emulsion of fat droplets in water. In a **cream separator**, the milk is spun fast and the lighter fat-rich cream collects towards the axis, leaving skim milk. In the traditional kitchen, curd or cream is **churned** with a wooden churner. The whirling motion makes fat droplets join into lumps of **butter**, which float, leaving buttermilk. The idea is like centrifugation: spinning and lighter fat.

visual.alt: Table comparing a cream separator, churning of curd and a blood centrifuge with the lighter and heavier parts

slides.narration: Milk is an emulsion of tiny fat droplets in water. In a cream separator, the milk is spun fast, and the lighter cream collects near the middle, leaving skim milk. In a kitchen, curd is churned with a wooden churner. The whirling makes fat droplets join into butter, which floats on buttermilk. The idea is similar to centrifugation, though churning joins the droplets together.

slides.heading: Sublimation, separating funnel and magnet
slides.body_md: **Sublimation:** some solids, such as ammonium chloride, camphor, naphthalene and iodine, turn straight into vapour on heating. Heat the mixture and the vapour re-forms as a solid on a cool surface. **Separating funnel:** two liquids that do not mix, such as oil and water, form layers; the denser lower layer is run off through the tap. **Magnetic separation:** a magnet pulls iron out of a mixture, as an electromagnet does in a scrap yard.

A separating funnel separates two liquids that do not mix, such as oil and water. The denser layer is run off through the tap. A magnet pulls out iron from a mixture, as in a scrap yard.

slides.heading: Winnowing, sieving and decantation
slides.body_md: **Winnowing:** a farmer tosses threshed grain into a breeze, and the lighter husk is blown away while heavier grain falls. **Sieving:** a sieve lets small particles through and keeps larger ones, as when atta is separated from coarse bran. **Sedimentation and decantation:** let a muddy mixture stand, the heavier solid settles, and then **pour off** the clear liquid above it.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Choose the method from the property that differs between the parts.
Evaporation leaves a dissolved solid behind (salt pans); crystallisation gives purer crystals on cooling (jaggery).
Simple distillation separates liquids with well-separated boiling points; fractional distillation needs a fractionating column.
Rf equals the distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent front.
Centrifugation, separating funnel, sublimation, magnet, winnowing, sieving and decantation use density, immiscibility, vapour, magnetism, weight, size and settling.

visual.alt: Table summarising the property that differs for each separation method

slides.narration: To sum up. Always choose a method from a property that differs. Evaporation leaves a dissolved solid, and crystallisation gives purer crystals on cooling. Simple distillation separates liquids with well separated boiling points, and fractional distillation uses a column when they are close. Chromatography uses speed on paper, and centrifugation uses density. Other methods use magnetism, weight, size and settling.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Draw distillation neatly: cold water enters at the lower end of the condenser and leaves at the upper end.
Always name the property that differs before naming the method.
Draw the chromatography base line with a pencil and give Rf the formula, with no unit.
Do not call churning pure centrifugation: say it is similar and that fat droplets join.
For traditional practices, link each step to a laboratory method.

notes.title: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Pure substances and mixtures
sections.body_md:
A **pure substance** (an element or a compound) has fixed composition and sharp, fixed properties such as a melting point. A **mixture** contains two or more substances mixed physically, in any proportion; each keeps its own properties, and the parts can be separated by physical methods.

- **Homogeneous mixture:** uniform throughout (sugar syrup, air without dust, brass, a solid solution).
- **Heterogeneous mixture:** composition varies and parts are often visible (muddy water, sand and iron filings, oil and water).

key_terms.definition_md: Matter of fixed composition: an element or a compound.
Two or more substances mixed physically in any proportion.
A mixture with uniform composition throughout.
A mixture whose composition varies from place to place.

visual.alt: Table sorting four mixtures into homogeneous and heterogeneous

sections.heading: 2. Solutions, suspensions and colloids
sections.body_md:
Particle size decides the kind of liquid mixture: below about 1 nm a **solution**, about 1 to 1000 nm a **colloid**, above about 1000 nm a **suspension**.

A solution and a colloid are stable and do not settle. A suspension settles, and its particles are held back by filter paper. A colloid passes through filter paper but **scatters light**: the **Tyndall effect**. A solution does not scatter light. Misty-morning sunbeams in a forest show the Tyndall effect.

key_terms.definition_md: A homogeneous mixture with particles below about 1 nm; clear and stable.
A mixture with particles about 1 to 1000 nm; stable, passes through filter paper, scatters light.
A heterogeneous mixture with particles above about 1000 nm that settle and are filtered off.
The scattering of a light beam by colloidal (or larger) particles, making its path visible.

sections.heading: 3. Types of colloid
sections.body_md: Colloids are named by the dispersed phase and the medium: **aerosol** (liquid or solid in gas: fog, smoke), **foam** (gas in liquid: shaving cream), **emulsion** (liquid in liquid: milk, face cream), **sol** (solid in liquid: ink, paint) and **gel** (liquid in solid: jelly, cheese).

A liquid spread in a solid, such as jelly.

sections.heading: 4. Concentration of a solution
sections.body_md:
The **solute** dissolves in the **solvent** to give the **solution**. Concentration can be stated as
$$\text{mass percentage} = \dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$$
$$\text{volume percentage} = \dfrac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}} \times 100$$
$$\text{mass by volume percentage} = \dfrac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (mL)}} \times 100$$
Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent. Example: 36 g sugar in 164 g water is 36/200 × 100 = 18 % by mass.

key_terms.definition_md: The amount of solute present in a given amount of solution.
Mass of solute in 100 g of solution.
Volume of solute in 100 mL of solution.
Grams of solute in 100 mL of solution.

sections.heading: 5. Solubility, saturation and crystallisation
sections.body_md:
**Solubility** is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. An **unsaturated** solution can dissolve more; a **saturated** one cannot. On a solubility curve, a point on the curve is saturated and a point below it is unsaturated.

For most solids, solubility **rises** with temperature (potassium nitrate steeply, sodium chloride very little), so cooling a hot saturated solution gives **crystals**. For gases, solubility **falls** as temperature rises. Example from the illustrative curve: 100 g of water saturated at 60 °C gives 110 − 32 = 78 g of crystals when cooled to 20 °C.

key_terms.definition_md: Maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature.
A solution holding the maximum solute at that temperature.
A solution that can still dissolve more solute at that temperature.
Formation of pure crystals from a hot saturated solution as it cools.

sections.heading: 6. Evaporation, crystallisation and distillation
sections.body_md:
**Evaporation** leaves a dissolved solid behind (the salt pans of Gujarat). **Crystallisation** purifies a solid and avoids charring (jaggery from boiled cane juice).

**Simple distillation** separates liquids with a large difference in boiling point (acetone 56 °C and water 100 °C); the condenser is cooled by water entering at the lower end. **Fractional distillation** uses a fractionating column for close boiling points (ethanol and water, liquefied air, petroleum). The traditional **deg and bhapka** of Kannauj use the same idea to make attars.

sections.heading: 7. Chromatography, centrifugation and other methods
sections.body_md:
**Paper chromatography** separates dyes or pigments by their speed on paper. The base line is drawn in pencil. $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent front}}$, between 0 and 1, with no unit.

**Centrifugation** flings denser particles to the bottom (cream separator, blood cells). **Churning** of curd makes butter by joining fat droplets. Also: **sublimation** (camphor, ammonium chloride), **separating funnel** (oil and water), **magnet** (iron filings), **winnowing** (husk and grain), **sieving** (atta and bran) and **decantation** (pour off the clear liquid).

key_terms.definition_md: Separation of substances that move at different speeds on a stationary phase.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Divide by the mass of the whole solution when finding a mass percentage.
- Prove a colloid by the Tyndall effect and by the fact that it does not settle.
- Read solubility curves with dashed guide lines and quote both values.
- Name the property that differs before naming the separation method.
- Draw distillation with cold water entering at the lower end of the condenser.
- Rf has no unit and lies between 0 and 1.

cards.front_md: What is a pure substance?
cards.back_md: Matter of fixed composition and fixed properties: an element or a compound.

cards.front_md: What is a mixture?
cards.back_md: Two or more substances mixed physically in any proportion; each keeps its properties.

cards.front_md: What is a homogeneous mixture?
cards.back_md: A mixture with uniform composition throughout, such as sugar syrup or brass.

cards.front_md: What is a heterogeneous mixture?
cards.back_md: A mixture whose composition varies; the parts can often be seen, such as muddy water.

cards.front_md: Is brass a compound or a mixture?
cards.back_md: A homogeneous mixture: a solid solution of copper and zinc.

cards.front_md: Particle size in a solution, a colloid and a suspension?
cards.back_md: Below about 1 nm; about 1 to 1000 nm; above about 1000 nm.

cards.front_md: Which of solution, colloid, suspension settles on standing?
cards.back_md: Only the suspension.

cards.front_md: Which mixtures pass through ordinary filter paper?
cards.back_md: Solutions and colloids; a suspension leaves a residue.

cards.front_md: What is the Tyndall effect?
cards.back_md: The scattering of a light beam by colloid particles, making its path visible.

cards.front_md: Does a true solution show the Tyndall effect?
cards.back_md: No; its particles are too small to scatter light.

cards.front_md: Why do sunbeams show up in a misty forest?
cards.back_md: Water droplets and dust scatter the sunlight: the Tyndall effect.

cards.front_md: What kind of colloid is fog? Milk? Jelly?
cards.back_md: Fog: aerosol. Milk: emulsion. Jelly: gel.

cards.front_md: What is shaving cream as a colloid?
cards.back_md: A foam: gas bubbles in a liquid.

cards.front_md: Formula for mass percentage?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$

cards.front_md: Formula for volume percentage?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}} \times 100$

cards.front_md: Formula for mass by volume percentage?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (mL)}} \times 100$

cards.front_md: 36 g sugar in 164 g water. Mass percentage?
What is solubility?
cards.back_md: The maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature.

cards.front_md: Saturated and unsaturated solution?
cards.back_md: Saturated: holds the maximum solute at that temperature. Unsaturated: can dissolve more.

cards.front_md: How does temperature affect the solubility of most solids and of gases?
cards.back_md: Solids: usually rises. Gases: falls.

cards.front_md: What gives crystals from a hot saturated solution?
cards.back_md: Cooling it: crystallisation.

cards.front_md: Which method gives salt on the Gujarat coast?
cards.back_md: Evaporation of sea water in shallow pans by sun and wind.

cards.front_md: Why prefer crystallisation to evaporating to dryness?
cards.back_md: It gives purer crystals and avoids charring heat-sensitive solids.

cards.front_md: When is simple distillation enough?
cards.back_md: When the boiling points differ by a large amount, such as acetone and water.

cards.front_md: When is fractional distillation used?
cards.back_md: For liquids with close boiling points, using a fractionating column.

cards.front_md: Where does cold water enter a Liebig condenser?
cards.back_md: At the lower end, and leaves at the upper end.

cards.front_md: What are the deg and the bhapka?
cards.back_md: The copper pot and the receiver of the traditional Kannauj attar still.

cards.front_md: Formula for Rf?
cards.back_md: $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent front}}$

cards.front_md: Why is the chromatography base line drawn in pencil?
cards.back_md: Pencil graphite does not dissolve and move with the solvent; ink would.

cards.front_md: What does centrifugation do?
cards.back_md: Spins a mixture so that denser particles go to the bottom as sediment.

cards.front_md: Name the property used: winnowing, sieving, magnet, sublimation.
cards.back_md: Weight, size, magnetism, and a solid turning straight into vapour.

questions.stem_md: Brass is made by melting copper and zinc together and letting the melt cool. Under a microscope it looks the same everywhere, and its copper to zinc ratio can be changed by the maker. Brass is:

options.text_md: a compound, because it looks uniform throughout
a heterogeneous mixture, because it contains two different metals
an element, because it is a metal
a homogeneous mixture (a solid solution), because its composition is uniform but not fixed

questions.solution_md: The ratio of the metals can be varied, so brass is a mixture, not a compound. It is uniform throughout, so it is homogeneous (a solid solution) — option (d). Looking uniform does not make a substance a compound, so (a) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: Which pair contains only homogeneous mixtures?

options.text_md: Muddy water and a vegetable salad
Sugar syrup and air that is free of dust
Granite and sugar syrup
Sand stirred in water and air free of dust

questions.solution_md: Sugar syrup and dust-free air are uniform throughout — option (b). Each other pair has at least one heterogeneous member: muddy water, salad, granite, or sand stirred in water.

questions.stem_md: Liquid L1 boils steadily at 78 °C throughout. Liquid L2 starts to boil at 82 °C, and the thermometer keeps rising to 96 °C as it boils away. The most likely conclusion is that:

options.text_md: L1 is a pure liquid and L2 is a mixture
L1 is a mixture and L2 is a pure liquid
both are pure liquids with different boiling points
both are mixtures of the same liquids

questions.solution_md: A pure liquid has a fixed boiling point, so L1 stays at one temperature. A mixture boils over a range as its composition changes, as L2 does — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement is NOT true of a mixture?

options.text_md: Its components can be present in any proportion
Its components keep their own properties
Its components can be separated by physical methods
It has a fixed melting point, like a pure substance

questions.solution_md: A mixture has no fixed melting point because its composition can vary, so the statement in (d) is false. The other statements are true of mixtures.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because muddy water settles when left to stand, it is a homogeneous mixture.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Muddy water has visible mud particles that settle, so its composition is not uniform: it is a heterogeneous mixture (a suspension).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Brass is classified as a homogeneous mixture.

**Reason (R):** Copper and zinc are always present in brass in one fixed ratio by mass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: brass is a solid solution, uniform throughout. R is false: the ratio can be varied (for example 70 : 30 or 60 : 40), which is why brass is a mixture — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Distilled water and sea water both look clear. Name the one that is a pure substance and give one test, using boiling, that tells them apart.

answer.model_answer_md: Distilled water is the pure substance. It boils at a fixed 100 °C at sea level, and the temperature stays steady while it boils. Sea water is a mixture, so it begins to boil at a slightly higher temperature, which keeps rising as water leaves and the salt gets more concentrated.

questions.solution_md: Distilled water is pure: fixed boiling point; sea water boils over a range.

marking_scheme.step: Fixed, steady boiling point of pure water
Sea water boils over a changing range

questions.stem_md: A torch beam is passed in a dark room through a tumbler of clear sugar solution and then through a tumbler of water with a little starch dispersed in it. In which will the path of the beam be seen, and why?

options.text_md: Only in the sugar tumbler, because dissolved sugar particles are the largest
Only in the starch tumbler, because the starch particles are large enough to scatter light
In both tumblers equally, because both are mixtures
In neither, because light cannot travel through a liquid

questions.solution_md: Colloidal starch particles scatter light, so the beam path shows up (the Tyndall effect). Sugar in solution has particles too small to scatter light — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A liquid mixture has particles about 200 nm across. It does not settle when left overnight, passes through ordinary filter paper and makes a torch beam visible. It is:

options.text_md: a colloid
a true solution
a suspension
a pure liquid

questions.solution_md: Particles of 1 to 1000 nm that do not settle, pass through filter paper and scatter light make a colloid — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On a misty morning, beams of sunlight can be seen slanting through the trees of a forest. This is because:

options.text_md: droplets and dust in the misty air scatter the sunlight, as in the Tyndall effect
the air molecules are large enough to settle and reflect light
light itself is visible as a solid rod when it passes through trees
the leaves of the trees emit light of their own

questions.solution_md: Mist is a colloid of tiny water droplets in air. Its particles scatter the sunlight so that the beam path shows — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A bottle of shaving cream, when pressed, gives a soft mass of gas bubbles spread through a liquid. This colloid is called:

options.text_md: an emulsion
a gel
a foam
an aerosol

questions.solution_md: Gas dispersed in a liquid is a foam — option (c). An emulsion is liquid in liquid, a gel is liquid in solid and an aerosol is liquid or solid in gas.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A suspension of chalk powder in water passes through ordinary filter paper without leaving any residue.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The chalk particles are larger than the pores of the paper, so they are held back as a residue.

questions.stem_md: The scattering of light by the particles of a colloid, which makes the path of a beam visible, is called the ___ effect.
questions.solution_md: This is the **Tyndall** effect.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The path of a torch beam is clearly visible in water to which a few drops of milk have been added.

**Reason (R):** The particles in the milk and water mixture are large enough to scatter light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the diluted milk is a colloid. R is true and it explains A, since particles of colloidal size scatter light — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student lists four colloids seen on a rainy day in the kitchen and market. Match each (Column A) with its type (Column B).

options.text_md: Thick fog over a highway
Foam on top of a cup of lassi
Fresh milk in a steel can
Wobbling fruit jelly in a bowl

questions.solution_md: Fog is liquid droplets in air (aerosol), the lassi foam is gas in liquid (foam), milk is liquid in liquid (emulsion) and jelly is liquid in solid (gel).

questions.stem_md: A torch beam shows its path in a tumbler of dilute milk but not in a tumbler of salt solution. Explain the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: Dilute milk is a colloid, whose particles are large enough to scatter light, so the path of the beam is visible. The particles of a salt solution are far smaller, less than a nanometre, so they cannot scatter the light and the beam passes through without being seen.

questions.solution_md: Colloid particles scatter light; solution particles are too small.

marking_scheme.step: Colloid particles are large enough to scatter light
Dissolved salt particles are too small to scatter light

questions.stem_md: A farmer filters muddy pond water and also filters a little milk through the same cloth. Which one leaves a residue, and why does the other pass through?

answer.model_answer_md: The muddy water leaves a residue, because it is a suspension whose particles are larger than the pores of the cloth. Milk is a colloid, whose particles are far smaller, so they pass through the pores of the cloth along with the liquid.

questions.solution_md: Suspension particles are retained; colloid particles pass through.

marking_scheme.step: Muddy water leaves a residue; its particles are bigger than the pores
Milk particles are colloidal and small enough to pass through

questions.stem_md: State three differences between a true solution and a suspension.

answer.model_answer_md: In a true solution the particles are smaller than a nanometre, while in a suspension they are bigger than a thousand nanometres. A solution is clear and does not settle, whereas a suspension is cloudy and its particles settle on standing. A solution passes through filter paper without leaving a residue, but a suspension leaves a residue on the paper.

questions.solution_md: Particle size, settling, filtration.

marking_scheme.step: Particle size: below 1 nm against above 1000 nm
Settling on standing: no against yes
Filter paper: no residue against residue

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student tests four liquids P, Q, R and S in a dark room with a torch. She also leaves each liquid for 30 minutes and then pours it through filter paper.

| Liquid | Appearance | Settles in 30 min? | Residue on filter paper? | Path of the beam |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | clear | no | no | not seen |
| Q | milky | no | no | clearly seen |
| R | cloudy brown | yes | yes | seen, but the liquid is cloudy |
| S | clear | no | no | not seen |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) a colloid, since it does not settle or leave a residue but scatters light

**(b)** P and S, because they are clear, do not settle, leave no residue and show no beam.

**(c)** (i) The brown particles would settle at the bottom as a layer, leaving a clearer liquid above. R is a suspension, because its particles are large and settle under gravity.

**OR** (ii) Q passes through the filter paper with no residue, because its particles are small. The Tyndall effect shows that Q is not a solution, since the beam path is visible in it.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Q does not settle and passes through the paper, so it is not a suspension. It scatters light, so it is not a true solution. It is a colloid — option (a).

**(b)** P and S show none of the three signs.

**(c)** (i) Particles settle; suspension.

(ii) It passes through; the Tyndall effect.

children.stem_md: Liquid Q is best described as:

options.text_md: a colloid, since it does not settle or leave a residue but scatters light
a suspension, since it looks milky
a true solution, since it does not settle
a pure compound, since it looks uniform

children.solution_md: Q does not settle and passes through the paper, so it is not a suspension. It scatters light, so it is not a true solution. It is a colloid — option (a).

children.stem_md: Which two liquids could be true solutions?

answer.model_answer_md: P and S, because they are clear, do not settle, leave no residue and show no beam.

children.solution_md: P and S show none of the three signs.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Liquid R is left undisturbed overnight. Describe what you would see and name the type of mixture.

answer.model_answer_md: The brown particles would settle at the bottom as a layer, leaving a clearer liquid above. R is a suspension, because its particles are large and settle under gravity.

marking_scheme.step: Particles settle to the bottom, clearer liquid above

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Liquid Q is poured through fine filter paper. Say what passes through, and name the test that shows it is not a solution.

answer.model_answer_md: Q passes through the filter paper with no residue, because its particles are small. The Tyndall effect shows that Q is not a solution, since the beam path is visible in it.

questions.stem_md: A bottle of antiseptic solution is labelled "5 % mass by mass". This means that it contains:

options.text_md: 5 g of solute in every 100 g of the solvent
5 g of solute in every 100 mL of the solvent
5 g of solute in every 100 g of the solution
5 mL of solute in every 100 g of the solution

questions.solution_md: Mass percentage is the mass of solute in 100 g of the whole solution — option (c). The solvent alone is not 100 g.

questions.stem_md: At a certain temperature 38 g of a salt dissolves at most in 100 g of water. Ravi dissolves 30 g of it in 100 g of water at that temperature. The solution is:

options.text_md: saturated, since the salt has dissolved completely
saturated, since 30 g is less than 38 g
unsaturated, since it can dissolve 8 g more
unsaturated, since it can dissolve 38 g more

questions.solution_md: The solubility is 38 g per 100 g of water. Since 30 g is less than 38 g, the solution can still take $38 - 30 = 8$ g more, so it is unsaturated — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Hot saturated solutions of potassium nitrate and of sodium chloride, each made with 100 g of water at 80 °C, are cooled to 20 °C. Using the approximate curves, why does the potassium nitrate solution give far more crystals?

options.text_md: Its solubility falls steeply as the temperature falls, while that of sodium chloride changes very little
Potassium nitrate is lighter and floats out of the solution
Sodium chloride is more soluble at 20 °C than at 80 °C
Both change by the same amount, but potassium nitrate is heavier

questions.solution_md: The potassium nitrate curve is steep, so a lot of it leaves the solution when cooled. The sodium chloride curve is almost flat, so very little crystallises — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Small bubbles form on the inside wall of a glass of cold tap water left in a warm kitchen. These are bubbles of dissolved air coming out because:

options.text_md: the solubility of a gas in water increases when the temperature rises
the water is evaporating very rapidly
the solubility of a gas in water decreases when the temperature rises
cold water cannot hold any gas at all

questions.solution_md: Gases become less soluble in water as it warms, so dissolved air is released as bubbles — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two sugar solutions are made. Solution P has 10 g of sugar in 90 g of water. Solution Q has 15 g of sugar in 135 g of water. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Both have the same mass percentage of sugar
Q is more concentrated, because it has more sugar
P is more concentrated, because it has less water
P is more concentrated, because it has more sugar per gram of water

questions.solution_md: P: $10 / (10 + 90) \times 100 = 10\ \%$. Q: $15 / (15 + 135) \times 100 = 10\ \%$. The two are equal — option (a), although Q has more sugar.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A solution of potassium nitrate that is exactly saturated at 40 °C becomes unsaturated if it is warmed to 60 °C with no water lost.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The solubility of potassium nitrate is higher at 60 °C, so the warmer solution can dissolve more and is no longer saturated.

questions.stem_md: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at a given temperature is called a ___ solution.
questions.solution_md: It is a **saturated** solution.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cooling a hot saturated solution of sodium chloride from 80 °C to 20 °C gives a large crop of crystals.

**Reason (R):** The solubility of sodium chloride in water changes very little with temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: because the solubility of sodium chloride hardly changes, only a few crystals appear. R is true and is the reason A is false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: For a batch of jalebi syrup, a halwai dissolves 120 g of sugar in 480 g of water. Find the mass percentage of sugar in the syrup.
questions.solution_md: Mass of solution $= 120 + 480 = 600$ g. Mass percentage $= 120 / 600 \times 100 = 20.0\ \%$.

questions.stem_md: A laboratory assistant must prepare 750 g of a 6 % (mass by mass) solution of sodium carbonate. How many grams of water are needed?
questions.solution_md: Mass of solute $= 6/100 \times 750 = 45.0$ g. Mass of water $= 750 - 45.0 = 705.0$ g.

questions.stem_md: A cleaning liquid is made by adding water to 88 mL of isopropyl alcohol until the total volume is 400 mL. Find the volume percentage of alcohol.
questions.solution_md: Volume percentage $= 88 / 400 \times 100 = 22.0\ \%$.

marking_scheme.step: Volume of solution is 400 mL, not the volume of water

questions.stem_md: A glucose drip bag contains 25 g of glucose dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution. Find the concentration as mass by volume percentage.
questions.solution_md: Mass by volume percentage $= 25 / 500 \times 100 = 5.00\ \%$.

marking_scheme.step: Solute in grams and solution in millilitres

questions.stem_md: Using the approximate solubility of potassium nitrate, 64 g per 100 g of water at 40 °C, find how many grams dissolve in 250 g of water to make a saturated solution at 40 °C.
questions.solution_md: 250 g of water is $250/100 = 2.5$ times 100 g, so mass dissolved $= 64 \times 2.5 = 160$ g.

marking_scheme.step: 250 g of water is 2.5 times 100 g

questions.stem_md: A saturated solution of potassium nitrate is made with 300 g of water at 60 °C. Using the approximate values 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 32 g per 100 g at 20 °C, find the mass of crystals that appear on cooling to 20 °C.
questions.solution_md: In 300 g of water: at 60 °C, $110 \times 3 = 330$ g; at 20 °C, $32 \times 3 = 96$ g. Crystals $= 330 - 96 = 234$ g.

marking_scheme.step: Dissolved at 60 °C and at 20 °C in 300 g of water: 330 g and 96 g

questions.stem_md: The approximate solubility of sodium chloride at 40 °C is 37 g per 100 g of water. Find the mass percentage of sodium chloride in a saturated solution at that temperature.
questions.solution_md: Mass of solution $= 100 + 37 = 137$ g. Mass percentage $= 37 / 137 \times 100 = 27\ \%$.

questions.stem_md: To obtain crystals from a solution, a student heats it until it is nearly saturated and then lets it cool slowly instead of boiling it dry. Give two reasons for this.

answer.model_answer_md: On slow cooling, the solubility falls and well-shaped pure crystals form while the impurities stay in the liquid. Boiling to dryness would leave the impurities mixed with the solid, and a heat-sensitive solid such as sugar could char.

questions.solution_md: Purer crystals; no charring.

marking_scheme.step: Cooling a saturated solution gives pure crystals, impurities stay dissolved
Boiling to dryness leaves impurities or may char the solid

questions.stem_md: A saturated solution of potassium nitrate at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. Using the shape of its solubility curve, explain what you will see and why. Say what happens if the solution had been unsaturated at 60 °C.

answer.model_answer_md: The solubility of potassium nitrate is much lower at 20 °C than at 60 °C, so the cooled solution can no longer hold all the solute, and the extra comes out as crystals. If the solution had been unsaturated at 60 °C, it may still hold everything at 20 °C, so crystals would form only if the cooling went far enough to reach saturation.

questions.solution_md: Lower solubility on cooling gives crystals; an unsaturated solution may give none.

marking_scheme.step: An unsaturated solution may stay clear until saturation is reached

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define solubility and distinguish between saturated and unsaturated solutions.

(b) A saturated solution of a salt is made with 100 g of water at 80 °C, where the solubility is 100 g, and is cooled to 20 °C, where it is 25 g. Find the mass of crystals.

(c) State how the solubility of a gas changes when the temperature rises, with one everyday observation.

answer.model_answer_md: Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. A saturated solution holds this maximum, so extra solute stays undissolved, while an unsaturated solution can dissolve more. In (b), the solution holds 100 g at 80 °C but only 25 g can stay dissolved at 20 °C, so 100 − 25 = 75 g of crystals form. In (c), the solubility of a gas falls as the temperature rises, so bubbles escape from a warm fizzy drink.

questions.solution_md: Definition and saturated against unsaturated; 100 − 25 = 75 g; gases less soluble on heating.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Definition of solubility and of saturated against unsaturated
(c) Gas solubility falls with a rise in temperature; example

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student measures how much of a salt X (a made-up salt for practice, so the values are given, not real) dissolves in 100 g of water at four temperatures.

| Temperature (°C) | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility of X (g per 100 g water) | 25 | 40 | 60 | 100 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) unsaturated, because up to 10 g more can still dissolve

**(b)** $40 \times 2.5 = 100$ g.

**(c)** (i) At 80 °C, 100 g dissolve; at 20 °C only 25 g can stay dissolved. Crystals $= 100 - 25 = 75$ g.

**OR** (ii) Mass of solution $= 100 + 100 = 200$ g, so the mass percentage $= 100 / 200 \times 100 = 50\ \%$.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The solubility at 60 °C is 60 g per 100 g of water. The solution holds 50 g, so $60 - 50 = 10$ g more can dissolve: it is unsaturated — option (d).

**(b)** Solubility 40 g per 100 g; 250 g is 2.5 times 100 g.

**(c)** (i) Crystals = 100 − 25 = 75 g.

(ii) Mass of solution 200 g; 100/200 × 100 = 50 %.

children.stem_md: At 60 °C the student stirs 50 g of X into 100 g of water. The solution is:

options.text_md: saturated, because 50 g has dissolved
unsaturated, because 60 g more can dissolve
saturated, because the temperature is 60 °C
unsaturated, because up to 10 g more can still dissolve

children.solution_md: The solubility at 60 °C is 60 g per 100 g of water. The solution holds 50 g, so $60 - 50 = 10$ g more can dissolve: it is unsaturated — option (d).

children.stem_md: How many grams of X dissolve in 250 g of water at 40 °C to make a saturated solution?
children.solution_md: Solubility 40 g per 100 g; 250 g is 2.5 times 100 g.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): A saturated solution of X made with 100 g of water at 80 °C is cooled to 20 °C. Find the mass of crystals formed.

answer.model_answer_md: At 80 °C, 100 g dissolve; at 20 °C only 25 g can stay dissolved. Crystals $= 100 - 25 = 75$ g.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Find the mass percentage of X in the saturated solution at 80 °C.

answer.model_answer_md: Mass of solution $= 100 + 100 = 200$ g, so the mass percentage $= 100 / 200 \times 100 = 50\ \%$.

questions.stem_md: Sea water is let into wide, shallow pans along the Gujarat coast. After some days a crust of common salt is raked up. Salt is obtained mainly by:

options.text_md: filtration of the sea water through sand
distillation using a condenser
sublimation of the salt
evaporation of the water by sun and wind

questions.solution_md: The sun and wind evaporate the water, leaving the dissolved salt behind — option (d). Sea water is not filtered to make salt, no condenser is used, and salt does not sublime.

questions.stem_md: Two liquids that mix completely boil at 78 °C and 82 °C. To separate them in a laboratory, the best method is:

options.text_md: simple distillation, because both are liquids
fractional distillation, because their boiling points are close
a separating funnel, because they form layers
centrifugation, because they have different densities

questions.solution_md: Close boiling points need a fractionating column — option (b). A separating funnel is only for liquids that do not mix, and centrifugation is for tiny suspended particles.

questions.stem_md: A Punjab farmer tosses threshed wheat into the air on a breezy day. The husk is blown aside and the grains fall in a heap. This works because:

options.text_md: the husk is heavier than the grains
the grains dissolve in moving air
the husk is lighter than the grains
the husk is attracted by a magnet

questions.solution_md: Winnowing depends on a difference in weight, so the breeze carries the lighter husk farther than the heavier grains — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student draws the starting line on chromatography paper with a pencil and not with an ink pen because:

options.text_md: graphite is heavier than the dyes being tested
graphite does not dissolve in the solvent and so does not move up the paper
ink spots are always larger than pencil spots
a pencil line is the only line the solvent can cross

questions.solution_md: Ink contains dyes that would dissolve and move with the solvent, confusing the result. Graphite stays put — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Four students report the Rf value of a spot in paper chromatography. Which report must be wrong?

options.text_md: 0.35, a spot that moved a little over a third of the way
0.80, a spot that moved most of the way
0.05, a spot that barely left the base line
1.3, because a spot cannot travel farther than the solvent front

questions.solution_md: Rf is the distance moved by the substance divided by that moved by the solvent front. The substance cannot go beyond the front, so Rf cannot exceed 1 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A blood sample is spun in a centrifuge in a pathology laboratory. The blood cells end up at the bottom of the tube because:

options.text_md: the lighter cells are thrown outward and sink to the bottom
the plasma evaporates quickly during the spinning
the spinning dissolves the cells in the plasma
the denser cells are thrown outward to the bottom, leaving the lighter plasma above

questions.solution_md: The spinning makes denser particles move to the outer end of the tube, which is the bottom — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A mixture of mustard oil and water forms two layers. Which technique separates the two liquids most simply?

options.text_md: Simple distillation of the whole mixture
A separating funnel, run off the lower layer through the tap
Filtration through filter paper
Sublimation by gentle heating

questions.solution_md: Immiscible liquids form layers; a separating funnel lets the denser lower layer be run off, leaving the upper layer — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In decantation, the clear liquid is poured off gently after the solid has settled at the bottom.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Decantation separates a settled solid from the liquid above it by pouring the clear liquid off.

questions.stem_md: The change of a solid directly into vapour on heating, as camphor or ammonium chloride does, is called ___.
questions.solution_md: This change is **sublimation**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The base line on a chromatography paper is drawn with a pencil.

**Reason (R):** The solvent rises through the paper and carries the dyes with it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true because pencil graphite does not dissolve. R is also true, but it does not explain why a pencil is used — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fractionating column is used to separate two liquids whose boiling points are close.

**Reason (R):** Vapour condenses and evaporates repeatedly in the column, getting richer in the more volatile liquid at each stage.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true and R is the working principle of the column, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A mixture of iodine and sand can be separated by sublimation.

**Reason (R):** Sand is insoluble in water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: iodine turns directly into vapour on heating, and sand does not. R is also true, but it is not why sublimation works — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A school science club has four separation tasks. Match each task (Column A) with the best method (Column B).

options.text_md: Separating the dyes in a black marker ink
Separating cream from fresh whole milk on a dairy farm
Separating kerosene from water
Recovering naphthalene balls mixed with sand

questions.solution_md: Dyes separate by speed on paper (chromatography); cream is lighter and is spun out (centrifugation); kerosene and water form layers (separating funnel); naphthalene vaporises on heating (sublimation).

questions.stem_md: In a paper chromatography experiment the solvent front rose 7 cm above the base line. A green spot was found 4.2 cm above the base line. Find its Rf value.

marking_scheme.step: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front

questions.stem_md: In a simple distillation set-up, the bulb of the thermometer is placed level with the side arm of the flask and not dipped in the boiling liquid. Why?

answer.model_answer_md: The thermometer must show the temperature of the vapour that is about to enter the condenser, which is the boiling point of the substance distilling over. A bulb dipped in the boiling mixture would read the temperature of the liquid, which can be higher.

questions.solution_md: It reads the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser.

marking_scheme.step: Thermometer should read the vapour temperature
The liquid can be hotter than the vapour distilling over

questions.stem_md: Explain how a farmer separates husk from threshed grain by winnowing. State the property on which the method depends.

answer.model_answer_md: The farmer tosses the mixture into the air on a breezy day. The wind blows the lighter husk away while the heavier grains fall nearly straight down into a heap. The method depends on the difference in weight between husk and grain.

questions.solution_md: Wind carries the lighter husk away; difference in weight.

marking_scheme.step: Mixture tossed in a breeze; husk blown away, grain falls
Depends on the difference in weight

questions.stem_md: A student states that the Rf value of a dye is 4.2 cm. Point out two errors in this statement.

answer.model_answer_md: Rf is a ratio of two distances, so it has no unit and cannot be given in centimetres. Also, an Rf value always lies between 0 and 1, so 4.2 is impossible: the spot cannot move farther than the solvent front.

questions.solution_md: Rf has no unit; it must be less than or equal to 1.

questions.stem_md: Describe how common salt is obtained from sea water in the salt pans of the Gujarat coast. Why is this method suitable for the place?

answer.model_answer_md: Sea water is let into wide, shallow pans. The sun and wind slowly evaporate the water, so the brine gets stronger until the salt separates as a crust, which is raked up, washed and dried. The method is suitable because the coast has plenty of sunshine and wind, so no fuel is needed.

questions.solution_md: Sea water in shallow pans; evaporation; crust raked; sun and wind.

marking_scheme.step: Sea water let into shallow pans
Sun and wind evaporate the water, salt crust forms
Salt raked up, washed and dried; uses sunshine, no fuel

questions.stem_md: In the traditional attar-making of Kannauj, flowers and water are heated in a copper deg and the vapour passes through a pipe to a bhapka in cool water. Name the separation method and match the two vessels to the parts of a laboratory set-up.

answer.model_answer_md: The method is distillation. The copper deg that holds the flowers and water is heated, so it acts as the distillation flask. The bhapka, standing in cool water, receives the vapour and condenses it, so it acts as the condenser and receiver, while the bamboo pipe is the delivery tube.

questions.solution_md: Distillation; deg as flask; bhapka as condenser and receiver.

marking_scheme.step: Deg is the heated distillation flask
Bhapka in cool water acts as condenser and receiver

questions.stem_md: Explain how a cream separator separates cream from milk. How is the churning of curd into butter like it, and how is it different?

answer.model_answer_md: A cream separator spins the milk very fast, so the denser skim milk is flung outward and the lighter fat-rich cream collects near the axis. Churning curd also whirls the liquid and the lighter fat comes out as butter. It differs because churning mainly makes the fat droplets join together into lumps of butter, while the separator sorts the milk by density.

questions.solution_md: Spinning; lighter cream near axis; churning joins droplets.

marking_scheme.step: Fast spinning throws denser skim milk outward, cream collects near the axis
Churning also whirls the mixture and fat floats as butter
Difference: churning joins the fat droplets

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the property that simple distillation depends on, and describe the apparatus in order from the flask to the receiver.

(b) Explain why cold water enters the condenser at its lower end.

(c) When is fractional distillation used instead? Give two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Simple distillation depends on a difference in boiling points. The mixture is heated in a flask with a thermometer at the side arm, the vapour passes into a sloping condenser, and the condensed liquid drips into the receiver. In (b), cold water enters at the lower end so that the jacket is always full and the vapour is cooled all along its length, with warm water leaving at the top. In (c), fractional distillation, with a fractionating column, is used when boiling points are close, as for ethanol and water or for the gases of liquefied air.

questions.solution_md: Boiling point; flask, side arm, condenser, receiver; cold water at the lower end fills the jacket; fractionating column for close boiling points.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Boiling point; flask, thermometer, condenser, receiver in order
(b) Cold water enters at the lower end and fills the jacket; warm water leaves at the top

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe how you would separate the dyes in a black ink by paper chromatography.

(b) Define Rf. A dye spot moved 3.0 cm while the solvent front moved 7.5 cm. Find its Rf.

(c) How would you decide if the ink contains a known dye?

answer.model_answer_md: In (a), a pencil base line is drawn near the bottom of the paper and a spot of the ink is placed on it. The paper is hung in a solvent with the base line above the solvent, and the solvent rises, carrying the dyes at different speeds until they form separate spots. In (b), Rf is the distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent front. Here Rf = 3.0 / 7.5 = 0.40. In (c), spot the known dye beside the ink and compare: the same Rf means the same dye.

questions.solution_md: Pencil base line; solvent rises; Rf = 3.0 / 7.5 = 0.40; compare with a known dye run alongside.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Pencil base line, spot, paper in solvent, dyes separate
(c) Compare with a known dye run alongside; same Rf

questions.stem_md: A science teacher gives three mixtures: (i) iron filings and sand, (ii) camphor and fine sand, (iii) oil floating on water. For each, name a method, the property it uses and one step of the procedure. Then say why simple filtration would fail for (i) and (ii) in this case.

answer.model_answer_md: For (i), a magnet separates the iron filings, because iron is magnetic and sand is not; the magnet is moved over the mixture. For (ii), sublimation is used, since camphor turns directly into vapour on heating while sand does not; the vapour is collected as solid on a cool surface above. For (iii), a separating funnel is used, because the two liquids form layers; the lower water layer is run off through the tap. Filtration fails for (i) and (ii) because there is no liquid, and both parts are solids.

questions.solution_md: Magnet, sublimation, separating funnel, each with property and step; no liquid for filtration.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Sublimation, because camphor turns to vapour directly
(iii) Separating funnel, layers run off through the tap
Filtration needs a liquid; (i) and (ii) are solid mixtures

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish a homogeneous mixture from a heterogeneous mixture, with one example each.

(b) A liquid does not settle, passes through filter paper and shows a bright beam in a dark room. Name its type and the effect you observed.

(c) Name two other differences between this liquid and a true solution.

answer.model_answer_md: A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition, as in sugar syrup, while a heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts, as in muddy water. In (b), the liquid is a colloid, and the bright beam is the Tyndall effect, caused by the particles scattering light. In (c), a colloid has particles of 1 to 1000 nm, which are larger than those of a true solution, and it scatters light, which a true solution does not, and it can be filtered only by very fine membranes like parchment.

questions.solution_md: Uniform against visible parts; colloid, Tyndall effect; particle size and light scattering.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: A student runs a black marker ink and four known dyes on one strip of chromatography paper. The solvent front rises 8.0 cm above the base line. The ink makes three spots, at 1.6 cm, 4.0 cm and 6.4 cm. The known dyes B, Y, G and R rise 1.6 cm, 4.0 cm, 5.2 cm and 6.4 cm respectively.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) G, because no ink spot is at 5.2 cm

**(b)** $R_f = 4.0 / 8.0 = 0.50$.

**(c)** (i) The Rf of Y stays 0.50, so its distance is $0.50 \times 10.0 = 5.0$ cm.

**OR** (ii) Pencil graphite does not dissolve, so it does not move up and interfere with the spots. The base line must be above the solvent, otherwise the spots would dissolve into the solvent in the container and be washed away.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The ink spots at 1.6, 4.0 and 6.4 cm match B, Y and R. None matches the 5.2 cm of G — option (b).

**(b)** Rf = 4.0 / 8.0 = 0.50.

**(c)** (i) Rf unchanged = 0.50; distance = 0.50 × 10.0 = 5.0 cm.

(ii) Graphite does not dissolve; spots would dissolve if the base line were under the solvent.

children.stem_md: Which known dye is NOT present in the black ink?

options.text_md: B, because it is the nearest to the base line
G, because no ink spot is at 5.2 cm
Y, because it is in the middle
R, because it moved the farthest

children.solution_md: The ink spots at 1.6, 4.0 and 6.4 cm match B, Y and R. None matches the 5.2 cm of G — option (b).

children.stem_md: Calculate the Rf of dye Y.
**Either** (i): The experiment is repeated until the solvent front rises 10.0 cm. At what height above the base line will dye Y be found?

answer.model_answer_md: The Rf of Y stays 0.50, so its distance is $0.50 \times 10.0 = 5.0$ cm.
